Darksiders: Warmastered Edition — Review
Darksiders: Warmastered Edition is a remastered version of the original action-adventure game, following War, one of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse. After being accused of bringing about the end of the world too soon, War returns to a devastated Earth to uncover the truth and clear his name.
The game blends hack-and-slash combat with exploration, platforming, and dungeon puzzles. War’s heavy weapons make battles feel powerful, while new abilities gradually open up more ways to fight and explore. The world is packed with ruined cities, demonic enemies, and striking fantasy designs.
The Warmastered Edition improves the visuals and performance, giving the original game a cleaner presentation. Some puzzles and mechanics feel dated, and the combat can become repetitive, but the mix of action and exploration remains enjoyable.
Verdict: Darksiders: Warmastered Edition is a stylish, satisfying adventure with a memorable setting. It’s worth a look for fans of dark fantasy and classic action games.

Darksiders 1 is one of the best Action-Adventure games (even for 2018).

** If you prefer a video review, check the bottom of this post ** 

This game has the typical premise of the war between Heaven & Hell but is packaged in a very interesting way by Vigil Games. Darksiders 1 is a an action-adventure and hack & slash game which has its share of platforming requirements and puzzles to solve. It's the first entry into the Darksiders series.

[b]PLOT[/b]
The background revolves around story of ancient factions vying for dominance over creation. There is Heaven and their supposed righteousness; Hell has its devious and destructive ways and there is the kingdom of Man who is the youngest of the different races. The Charred Council balances power among the races and ensures none of the older races or kingdoms gains an advantage until the Man is ready for the final apocalyptic battle. 

The union of some of the angels and demons resulted in the Nephilim. These were beings of power unto themselves. In game we find out why they were driven to a destructive crusade and we also learn that 4 of the Nephilim grew tired of the endless slaughter. These 4 deviants presented themselves before the Charred Council, swore servitude to uphold the balance between the factions. In exchange, they were given power and were soon known as the four horsemen. The destroyed the crusade of the Nephilim and slew their own brethren. Their power and belief in the balance of things kept the factions in check. With the relative balance set, the horsemen withdrew until the 7 seals in all of creation were to be broken which would signal the end of days and the final battle.

It is the supposed breaking of the seals that sets the tone for War's appearance in a war ravaged earth. It is here that War is held accountable for the supposed triggering of the End War. It is here, stripped of this formidable powers, that he journeys to find those responsible for igniting the Apocalyptic battle. It is here, the player is introduced to the youngest and brooding horseman War and his task of clearing his name.

[b]GRAPHICS & AUDIO[/b]
I did finish the Warmastered version of the game but the difference between the 2016 and the 2010 release is only minimal at best. Still the overall graphics of the game holds up in 2018. It won't make you feel like you were playing a very dated game. Its age does show in the environment aspect since some of the textures could still use additional work but its characters and NPCs are still very good looking. The demons in the game particularly show much better detail opposed to their angelic counterparts.

The spell effects are still good for the current year but they won't be as flashy as Darksiders 2 which is understandable. The Chaos Form, which is War's OP version of himself, is particularly un-impressive when compared to Death's Reaper Form in Darksiders 2. 

In terms of the audio, Darksiders is all around pleasing to the ears. The sounds lend well to the combat sequences and the background music is intense and fits the reality that Vigil Games is trying to tell. War's voice acting is top notch and gives that dark and defiant vibe. If you're a World of Warcraft player, you should recognize it as being very similar to Illidan's voiceover. That's the work of Liam O'Brian.

By the way, the cutscenes in the game are awesome.

[b]GAMEPLAY: GENERAL[/b]
Until you eventually get to use Ruin, War's steed, the movement around the gameworld can feel a tad slow. Even though the dash ability is something you can spam, the pause at the end of the dash animation is a bit lengthy. Once you get Ruin though and provided you are in a location that allows its use, it's a welcome companion as your attacks are also powered up.

The game does allow fast travel through Vulgrim's waypoint system which also serves as the game's shop. Using the waypoint system transports you to a limbo type world where you have to cross certain steps which I found weird and unnecessary. The locations of these waypoints are however convenient particularly in the first part of the game as there is a location you often have to re-visit. 

As a shop system, Vulgrim (an interesting character in himself by the way) sells you some of the different abilities you can use with the different weapons you can use in the game. He also sells 2 of the weapons used by a fellow horseman.The currency for his wares are in the form of souls which can be found from chests, inanimate objects (with the proper weapon enhancement) and killing mobs. About the soul system, the green souls have a different effect in that they help regenerate health and the yellow ones act as a resource for some of your "Wrath" abilities. It's an overall useful and un-complicated system.

Outside of combat, you do have to solve puzzles and jump and time movements to get through certain obstacles. The puzzles in the game are not in level of games like Uncharted but it doesn't mean you can go into it in a drunken state. The platforming activities are fun although War seems like a very unwieldy given the bulkiness of his character. It's sometimes weird seeing War glide in the air or swinging through chasms using his hook ability.

[b]GAMEPLAY: COMBAT[/b]
The combat in this game is very satisfying although the effects and finisher animations aren't all too flashy. As with any action game, being surrounded is a bad thing for your character but War is equipped with multiple abilities to help him "get out" or mow down his enemies. Knock back skills are important as in most games and your character has them. It doesn't work on some of the smaller mobs though so that's something to keep in mind.

War is very good in either single target or area-of-effect attacks. It will ofcourse depend on whether you have the right gear and purchased the appropriate upgrades from Vulgrim. If you're abilities and skills seem to be tickling your enemies instead of making them bleed, maybe it's time to consider spending some of your blue souls. 

Boss fights often require figuring out their mechanics before you can deal any damage to them. Thankfully, it becomes the norm that the new abilities or skills you learn in that section of the game means they should be useful against big bads. It just becomes a matter of determining when and how to use them. I've been in two boss fights where I spent 20-30 minutes figuring out how I can deal damage to them. It can be frustrating but once you figure it out, it becomes a breeze to complete a fight.

[b]SUMMARY[/b]
This game should be part of any action fan's library and especially if there is any intention of completing Darksiders 2 and eventually purchasing Darksiders 3. If it's your first time into the genre, this game will make you wonder why you didn't get into it sooner.

[quote][h1]TL;DR[/h1]
[spoiler]Darksiders is a compelling action adventure with God of War (I - III) style combat, and Legend of Zelda style progression, all with puzzles, gadgets and a catchy "Mystery Sound".

It combines infamous Joe "MAD" Madureira's unique and over-the-top art-style (Battle Chasers: Nightwar) with an epic story about the Apocalypse being kicked off too early and one of the four Horsemen being blamed for it. You take control of said rider, War, as he tries to uncover who is behind this conspiracy and cuts down Angels and Demons alike to get there. With its colorful yet brutal art-style, its epic soundtrack and its superb voice-acting (including Liam O'Brien and [b]Mark Hamill[/b]) this game is an instant recommendation. The Warmastered Edition is the same with more graphical options and the Harvester integrated instead of obtained via code.[/spoiler][/quote]

[h1][i]»War! Are you here to play executioner? They should have sent all four of you.«[/i][/h1]

Deceived by unknown forces of evil into prematurely riding on the Earth during what seemed like the End War, War – the first Horseman of the Apocalypse – stands accused of breaking the sacred law by inciting a war between Heaven and Hell. With the Demons victorious, the Earth now lays in ruins and humanity is all but extinct. Accused and dishonored, facing a fate far worse than death, War gets a chance to return to the Kingdom of Man a century later to make things right. Hunted by vengeful Angels, surrounded by bloodthirsty Demons, War mus make uneasy alliances with Demons, Angels and more ancient races if he wishes to succeed.

Can he destroy the Destroyer, restore the balance, uncover and convict the ones truly responsible and regain his honor?

[h1]🎮 Gameplay[/h1]

The core gameplay in Darksiders consists of [b]combat[/b], [b]exploration[/b] and [b]puzzle solving[/b]. It very obviously and very deliberately immitates and perfects these aspects from other well-known franchises.
[list]
[*][b]Combat[/b]
Telling you the combat wasn't inspired by the first [i]God of War[/i] games would be a blatant lie but Darksiders manages to pay hommage while perfecting it. Blows are impactful, War's growls are rough and as manly as Kratos' and there are very similar combinations, launchers, air-combinations and so on. As you progress in the story, you come across three weapon categories, starting with the huge sword Chaos Eater. Very early on you can unlock the quasi-optional Scythe (either a regular one or the much more expensive but also more powerful scythe of Death, "Harvester") and at a later point, you get powerful gauntlets, similar to the Nemean Cestus obtained in God of War III, offering a nice variety. Much like Kratos' Chains of Athena/Chaos, Chaos Eater is always equipped, while you can choose which of the other two is your current secondary weapon with a single button press, keeping the combat fast-paced and fluid.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1937919278

[*][b]Exploration[/b]
Much like in the early [i]The Legend of Zelda[/i] games and/or the [i]Metroidvania[/i] subgenre, parts of the interconnected World only become accessible later when you have defeated certain bosses and/or cleared certain dungeons and thus obtain new gadgets and abilities, forcing you to return to already visited areas multiple times to open up new branches of the world. Additionally there are several types of collectibles that can increase War's Health, Wrath (basically Mana) and budget or, in the case of the Abyssal Armor pieces, give him a new skin and a much higher armor rating. Some of these collectibles are hidden away quite well and also require a certain ability or gadget that you do not have on your first visit to the place. Since coming back to previously "cleared" branches of the world is highly optional, you will not find every collectable unless you go out of your way to look for them. As such the exploration can be highly rewarding.

[*][b]Puzzles[/b]
As I mentioned above, there are several dungeons in this game and each of them contains multiple puzzle rooms that require a combination of all the skills you have acquired thus far. With more abilities and gadgets unlocked the combinations required to solve each puzzle get more and more tricky. Much like in the [i]Legend of Zelda[/i] games, you get rewarded not only by being able to progress further but also by a "Mystery Sound" that is very recognizable and satisfying to hear.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1937918291[/list]

[h1]📖 Story / Presentation[/h1]

Eons ago a pact has been forged between the forces of Heaven and Hell to lay down their weapons until such a time when the Third Kingdom, the Kingdom of Man, is ready for the End War to determine the victor once and for all. To uphold the pact and thus the Balance, seven Seals have been forged to be broken upon the appointed time. Making sure that both sides honor the treaty are the feared Horsemen of the Apocalypse. [i]Darksiders[/i] begins when the Apocalypse hits 2010 Earth - many centuries too early. Both Demons and Angels are battling in the streets as terrified humans try to hide and run away and get slaughtered by the thousands. War, Rider of the Red Horse arrives on Earth, heeding the Call, fighting Demons and Angels alike. But something is amiss. The other Horsemen aren't present. War's powers are stripped away and he is defeated by an Archdemon. He learns that the Seals are still intact and that the Call wasn't sounded. Since he rode to Earth, alone to say the least, he gets accused of triggering the premature apocalypse himself.

A century after the Apocalypse started he returns to the ravaged Earth to discover who framed him and to prove his innocence to the Council, the entity that controls the Horsemen. A captivating story of intrigues, deception and powerstruggles starts to unfold with War in the center of it all.

[h1]🎼 Soundtrack[/h1]

Epic! Need I say more? In all seriousness, the score Chris Velasco created pulls you in from the moment you first see and hear the main menu theme.

[h1]💻 Graphics / Art-style[/h1]

The visuals look beyond decent even by today's standards thanks in no small part to the stylized art-style Joe "MAD" Madureira has created. This apocalypse is quite the colorful one and that's refreshing to say the least. Character designs are also beautiful with glowing, shining and gleaming details everyhwere and just a hint of that WoW aesthetic that fits in really well. Additionally, the game's intro and end cinematics are told via hand-drawn animations accompanied by a voice-over, which is a nice touch and works really well, especially in the beginning, when the pseudo-mythological aspects are explained.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1970673856

[h1]💰 Business Model[/h1]

[quote][u]Classic:[/u]
Buy the game, play the game.
No paid DLCs, items, lootboxes.[/quote]

[h1]📋 Conclusion[/h1]

Darksiders is not only an hommage to some other great games but also managed to create its own identity, lore and fanbase and spawn its own franchise that even survived studio closures and bankruptcies. With its timeless art-style, its superb voice-acting (featuring Mark Hamill), its intriguing and charismatic characters and the amazing franchise it is a part of, this has become a classic among the games and a bit of a masterpiece. If you've somehow managed to miss this game, do yourself a favor and try it.

[b] This review is MY opinion, MY own personal experience and MY thoughts. I am brutally honest when it comes to reviewing games. If you do not like my opinion, my time or respect my personal experience, please move on. [/b] 

[h1][b] A little bit of history [/b][/h1] 
Back in 2010 THQ wanted to make 4 Darksiders games, 1 for each horseman of course. Sadly, THQ filled for bankruptcy in 2011 which left us with Darksiders and Darksiders 2. It's an interesting mix.  It's got a little Legend of Zelda, some God of War, a bit of Doom, and a sprinkling of Diablo, all blended together in a Spawn-McFarlane-esque style.  The over-arching plot is a little cliche, but what happens on a plot point to plot point basis keeps things interesting.  War is basically the stereotypical "tough guy", but the supporting cast is what really steals the spotlight.

The game starts off slow, but after collecting more weapons and abilities while progressing through the storyline, the pace of combat becomes more frantic.  The depth of the world building also becomes deceptively more intricate.  I'm happy with the purchase and I've been enjoying it quite a lot.

If there's one absolute positive I can give Darksiders, it's that it finally cemented in my head exactly why Steam's review system is the way it is. Before, I've had frustration with how you can only give a 100 percent positive or 100 percent negative score. However, that score is contextualized as "recommended" or "not recommended." Do you think other people should play this game, or not?

Darksiders has a bit of a reputation of being a mishmash of different games- Zelda dungeons and puzzles, DMC combat, the Portal gun, etc. This is hardly a black mark on the game- there's no such thing as originality, after all. However, it's truly shocking how every single thing it borrows is not a remix, but an inferior copy. It has special moves like stingers, launchers, and strong attacks, but they're very clunky to chain together and create any combo more expressive than "ground combo, launch, air combo, slam back into ground," mixed with the hookshot when you get it. 

And yes, there is a hookshot equivalent, as well as a boomerang equivalent, a Portal Gun, etc. The hookshot is actually pretty versatile- it attaches to two different types of hooks, but also allows you to quick-attach to climbable walls and grapple enemies back to you for extended combos. However, that's as creative as the subweapons get. Most of them have no combo potential at all, and the only idea they had to keep the gun from being abusable was to make most strong enemies and bosses immune to it.

That's basically all the problems with this game in a nutshell- everything is sectioned off into its own little box, used for one purpose, every puzzle with one solution, regimented and segmented. Only place portals on the designated portal targets, only hit this enemy with this attack.

Even the story has problems with being generic- Christian theology with the serial numbers filed off so as not to offend the American Evangelical playerbase, war between heaven and hell, the Balance, the Destroyer, the Common Noun with Capital Letters so it Sounds Unique, the hordes of joyless scowling asshats with massive pauldrons. You've seen this game's story before. I almost wouldn't care about spoiling it, if I could bring myself to point out any specific plot element.

With all the problems this game has (like repeating one of the worst bosses three times, or having the final quest before the final boss being a fetch quest), it's not a bad game, per se. Or at least, it's not the worst game I've reviewed. It's actually better than some games that I've reviewed positively. However, we come back to the issue- to recommend or not recommend. Out of stubbornness or something, I played this game to completion, and I can tell you in the end that I really didn't think it was worth it. 

While entertaining at points, there is absolutely no reason to play this when you could be playing a game with better combat like Bayonetta or DMC, or better exploration like Breath of the Wild, or a more unique story like Fallout. And if you think those are some pretty normal-sounding recommendations, that's because this game is so unremarkable that you don't need to dig that hard to find something more interesting. You could also play something more interestingly bad, like Sudeki or MadSpace, if you want something off the beaten path. But there's no reason to play Darksiders. Not Recommended.

Darksiders Warmastered Edition is a really good and enjoyable game.  I had bought Darksiders several years ago and beat the game.  Several parts of the game play and story were very memorable, so when the Warmastered Edition was released and given for free to existing Darksiders owners, I thought it would be a good opportunity to play the game again.  Additionally, after looking through the achievements, it looked like most of them, if not all of them, could be completed during a standard play-thorough.  Complete it I did with only one or two achievements really requiring any extra effort.  The extra effort involved required just a little bit of backtracking through already visited areas to complete the collectibles, and riding Ruin for 100 miles, which I did AFK (the strategy with the Spirit Bridge was the most effective for me).

The story revolves around one of the Four Horseman of the Apocalypse, War.  The lore of this story line shows us that the Four Horseman are bound by laws established, from what I can tell, between Heaven and Hell and are only activated when the Final Battle for the world has started.  They are a "police force" who maintain the balance and despence justice against throse who break the rules, I guess.  Feared by all.  Somehow the final battle is "started" before it's time and before mankind has matured enough to take part.  War witnesses the beginning of the end of man and his actions against the minions of Heaven and Hell during the apocalypse result in his imprisonment by The Council.  War is charged with breaking the "rules"  and for his actions allowing Hell to grab an unfair advantage and, for the most part, win the Final Battle.  War is tasked with atoning for his sins and removing Hell's influence/control.  Thus War starts his quest to prove his innocence and seek revenge on those who used him.

I really loved this story.  Although some of it is a little confusing when I start looking at it in more detail, the epic feeling of the story is amazing and turned me into a real fan of the game series.  In the first few minutes of the game War fights with all his power, fighting through the streets of a city at the start of the Final Battle.  Buildings collapsing around him and people running in fear as Heaven and Hell fight through the streets.  Once sent on his path to prove his innocence, it is 100 years later, mankind is dead, cities destroyed, some areas turned to deserts of barren ash, etc.  As War traverses these areas fighting the undead, demons, and demonic super powered bosses.

For the most part, the game is fairly linear with some backtracking for collectible items that were once in-accessible, but can be accessed later once the proper weapon or tool becomes available to War later in the story.  Even though it is fairly linear, the developers really made Darksiders feel like an open world game that I could explore even though I really can't.  Unlike many games that take place pre-dominantly " confined and indoors" and are themselves linear, closed world games.  Those games actually feel linear, whereas Darksiders feels open because the world appears to continue on even when I reach a chasm that I can't cross or hit that "invisible map/zone wall."

For example, in the first area I enter after War's judgment, The Crossroads, down one of the streets is a big hole.  There is a chest in the hole that War can get to and climb out, but I can't cross to the other side.  When I awaken/free the Gate Guardian in the area to open up the next area, I can watch the Guardian walk to said pit, jump across it and continue walking down the street to disappear around the corner of a ruined building (that effect is used a few times).   I've beaten the game three times at this point and I still watch every Gate Guardian disappear into the distance.  

Also Darksiders doesn't just conveniently place destroyed buildings and such to act as "map/zone walls."  There are tons of areas what use "invisible" zone walls but continue to show the desolate, ruined world as far as the eye can see.  True, hitting the invisible walls may break the feel of an open world, but at the same time the developers don't put things up against these walls to encourage me to run into them.  So if I don't try to hit the zone walls, I can't tell they are there.  To further help the open world feel is that while War may stop when when he runs into a zone wall, if I pick up any environment objects like a car and throw it toward the wall, the car would keep flying into the distance.  Additionally, most zone walls are in spots that would be bottomless chasms anyways. All these effects really gave the game a truly epic feel.

Finally, as for the game play.  The game play is fun, fast and frenetic.  The most powerful weapon will always be War's sword, Chaos Eater.  He eventually gets a Scythe and the Tremor Gauntlet (think earthquakes).  While the sword is the strongest, the Tremor Gauntlet was more fun to use.  War ends up with a ton of useful tools and while most of them help him traverse parts of some levels, almost all of them can be used in battle for some amusing and creative fighting strategies.

When deciding to complete the game, one of the achievements is beating the game on Apocalyptic mode, and after reading how much damage monsters do (mid level mob hits take a full life bar) and requiring a lot more dodging (dodging is a play style weakness for me), I chose to do most of the achievements on Normal as well as re-learn boss strategies and collect the Abyssal Armor (War is almost to the final boss by the time it's completed) for Apocalyptic mode.   With all that done, Apocalyptic mode ended up being easier (in some ways) than normal with the Abyssal Armor.  I took less damage with the armor in hard mode than I did without it in normal mode, I think.  In hard mode play through, I didn't die once in battle the whole game, whereas I started dying to bosses around Silithus (spider boss) in Normal.  All deaths were from falling into lava, pits, etc.  Admittedly, I had figured out the strategies and gotten really good at dodging too, so...

I am not a heavy re-play person, but I enjoyed Darksiders so much when I bought it that the release of the Warmastered Edition peaked my interest in replaying.  I then beat the Warmastered Edition 2 more times and enjoyed the game more each time.  The End scene after the final boss gave me goose bumps every time and made me sad that Death's story in Darksiders 2 was the final game.  This is one series I truly wish got completed.

TLDR:  Great graphics, beautiful imagery, a semi-linear game that feels open world with an epic feel.  Great Story and Lore.  Good, useful weapons.  Fast and fun combat.  Worth It!

This game is worth a Steam Sale, and even regular price really.  I say that because if a 3rd game ever got released, I'd likely pay full release price instead of waiting for years for the cost to drop.

[h1]"In times of war, the law falls silent."
[i]~Marcus Tullius Cicero[/i][/h1]

The seventh generation of video game consoles. In my humble opinion, it was the last generation, in which console war was still a thing. I mean, seriously. Look at the world we live in now. We have [b]Kingdom Hearts[/b] and [b]Final Fantasy[/b] on [b]Xbox[/b], [b]Crash Bandicoot[/b] and [b]Forza[/b] on [b]PC[/b] and so on. Sure, technically, the console war is still on and some titles are still available only on certain platforms, but all in all, seventh generation was the last one when it was still interesting. The last one when it was actually worth having more than one system on you. And this game? It's taking advantage of that.

See, even up to this day we never had [b]The Legend of Zelda[/b] game outside [b]Nintendo[/b]'s system. We also never had [b]God of War[/b] game outside [b]PlayStation[/b] family. [b]Vigil Games[/b] decided to change that. Not by porting those games, of course (we all know what [b]Nintendo[/b] does with those who mess with their property, the guys are worse than any inquisition), but by making their own high quality alternative. That's pretty much all you need to know about the [b]Darksiders[/b]. It's stylish and charming mix between [b]The Legend of Zelda[/b] and [b]God of War[/b].

[b]Vigil Games[/b] didn't stop there, though. They literally took everything that was cool about popular titles like [b]Devil May Cry[/b], [b]Gungrave[/b], [b]Ubisoft[/b]'s [b]Prince of Persia[/b], [b]Legacy of Kain[/b], [b]Portal[/b] and even [b]WarCraft[/b] (design in this game was copied from what we had in [b]WarCraft III[/b] / [b]World of WarCraft[/b] almost as is), mixed all that together and called it a day. Sure, it doesn't sound that good. I mean... we all hate plagiarism, right? But you know what? It actually [i]is[/i] a good thing. Thanks to [b]Darksiders[/b], a lot of people who never played such games before finally got a chance to do so, while the others? The others just got even more of a good thing.

Like I said, [b]Darksiders[/b] is a high quality product. It looks good and it feels good. Almost as good as the original titles. And all of those different elements from different games? They work surprisingly well together. While playing as a brutal guy who looks almost exactly like [b]Arthas Menethil[/b], we'll explore a [b]Zelda[/b]-like world with dungeons, use a gun like [b]Dante[/b] and [b]Beyond the Grave[/b], do some basic tricks like in those early [b]Prince of Persia[/b] titles from [b]Ubisoft[/b], we'll fight some huge enemies and do [b]QTE[/b] like in [b]God of War[/b], solve the puzzles similar to what we had in [b]Zelda[/b], [b]Legacy of Kain[/b] and [b]Portal[/b], and so on. It really does work perfectly well. The addiction, the satisfaction... it's all here.

Add the fact that this game also comes with surprisingly great cast (not only we've got [b]Troy Baker[/b], we've also got [b]Mark Hamill[/b] himself, so, it's, like, one heck of a [b]Joker[/b] paradise here) and you'll see that... well... this game is good. Simple like that. You want a good game? Here it is. It's really hard to find something really bad to say about the [b]Darksiders[/b]. No matter how you look at it, it's a good game and that's it. Even the fact that [b]Vigil Games[/b] kind of overdid it with puzzles at one point can't change that (even though they sure did and this game comes with even more annoying dungeon than that [b]Water Temple[/b] thingy from [b]Ocarina of Time[/b], keep that in mind if you don't have enough patience).

There's one thing, though, that gives [b]Darksiders[/b] a certain... unpleasant aftertaste. I'm talking, of course, about the fact that this game doesn't have a face. Like [b]John Travolta[/b] in that certain [b]John Woo[/b] movie. Sure, it looks very impressive and stylish, but at the same time, when you look at this game? You don't see [b]Darksiders[/b]. You see the original games. When you watch cutscenes? It's a bloody [b]WarCraft[/b]. When you shoot? You see [b]Dante[/b]. When you pick up bombs from the ground? You see [b]Link[/b] who's getting ready to face [b]King Dodongo[/b]. And so on. The biggest problem with this game is that it can't really offer you anything unique, while everything that [b]Vigil Games[/b] borrowed from the other titles is so obvious that it's literally impossible not to think about that. It's just a bunch of some really cool stuff from the other, more famous titles and that's it. Does it ruin the game? Of course, not. And yet, like I said, it adds a certain unpleasant aftertaste. Like... you know. When you're playing one of those so-called “clones”, no matter how good it is, it's still just a clone, right?

There was a good chance to fix all that through story, bu-u-ut... let's just say that story is not the strongest point here. All in all, it's fine, but it relies too much on setting. You know, angels, demons, post-apocalyptic future... In other words, it's [b]Requiem: Avenging Angel[/b]. Which is pretty cool and stylish, but... let's just say that the actual storytelling is not really that good. [b]Vigil Games[/b] tried to follow the [b]God of War[/b] formula, in which our character just keeps beating the heck out of one character after another, but... let's just say that without [b]Kratos[/b] and his charisma you can't help but want more twists. I'm not trying to say that [b]War[/b] (yes, we're playing as one of the Horsemen of the Apocalypse here, because... you know... [b]War[/b]... [b]God of War[/b]... good grief...) isn't a charming character. It's just... it doesn't make as much impact as [b]Kratos[/b]. At least, not enough to cover for the lack of plot twists. In other words, the story just can't cover the fact that this game is just a clone. Unfortunately.

Then again, for those of us who don't have any consoles on them, this game is a great choice. And even for those who already played all of the games I've mentioned above, I can still recommend this one. Because, let's just admit it, having a good clone from time to time? It's a good thing. Like, OK, [b]Age of Empires[/b] is a good game. But it doesn't mean that we can't enjoy clones like [b]Star Wars: Galactic Battlegrounds[/b], [b]War Diary II[/b] and even [b]BC Kings[/b] because why the heck not? And [b]Darksiders[/b]? It's sure a good clone. Seriously, guys, you haven't played it yet? Go buy it.

[b]P.S.[/b] A couple of words about this exact version of the game, so-called [b]Warmastered Edition[/b] and what makes it different from the original. The new version comes with the [b]4K[/b] resolution support (in the original version you can't go higher than [b]2K[/b]), high resolution textures, improved shadows and post-processing effects, re-rendered cutscenes and, the best of all, the pre-order weapon (the [b]Harvester[/b] scythe) as a free bonus. Well, it won't be [i]free[/i], since you'll need to buy it with the in-game currency, but you know what I mean. In [b]Warmastered Edition[/b] you won't need any pre-order codes to get [b]Harvester[/b]. In other words, it's, like, the same exact thing, only better and with pre-order bonus as a gift. Which makes purchasing the original version kinda useless. As long as you're not a die-hard geek who wants to have every single version of this game. Dixi.

A solidly designed zelda-like that offers robust 3D combat, platforming, and a variety of environmental puzzles. The game has all the trademark gaming tropes of 2010 but stands as a testament to their well rounded implementation creating a rich well-crafted gaming experience that uses the whole cow.

The hack and slash gameplay gives you an interesting variety of weapons and attacks that have a hefty satisfying feel as you pummel enemies and smash up the environment with moves that really emphasise War's bulky strength. There's a ton of enemies to churn through but thankfully the God of War/DMC style combos, dashes, grabs, and finishers don't grow old with the later unlocks add new life to the combat throughout. Enemies are also well designed with a good variety of tactics and defences that force you to make full use of your weapons and attacks.

The areas are linear by today's standards but they have an openness that still feels like you have plenty of room for exploration. This is complimented by the movement options which include wall climbing, double jump and glide, horse riding, and later on the portal tool gives you access to distant and hidden corners. This was a time when they were maximising use of the limited space available.

Many of the gadgets you collect are primarily for solving puzzles but they also assist in combat as ranged weapons, or for repositioning adding further depth to the hefty combat system. The puzzles grow in complexity and the first tools remain in use up to the end of the game as mechanics are layered and woven together in later dungeons without feeling like it gets overdesigned.

Gameplay is mixed up between the usual free roaming exploration in the overworld, the interior dungeon levels that grant new tools/weapons ending with a boss fight, on rails shooter sections, and artillery style shooting gallery sections. This kind of gameplay variety wasn't as common and set the standard for a lot of this 3D action platformer style gameplay going forward.

This is one of those games that just implements everything with such fine tuning. It's a best in genre and a rare case of doing Zelda gameplay better than some of the Zelda games did. The combat, dungeons, puzzles, and bosses are fun, interesting, and make use of all the gear. The overworld is littered with its own puzzles and mysteries to unravel. The animation really puts war's heft and weight into every action, and the cartoony art style doesn't distract from the over-the-top spectacles of the angels, demons, and monsters you fight along the way.

A rare case of excellent design, fun setting, and great visuals. The music isn't very memorable however and the story is a bit convoluted, but those are small flaws in a well crafted game.

DARKSIDERS WARMASTERED EDITION – The First Horseman of the Apocalypse Returns!

"The balance between Heaven and Hell has been broken, who will pay the price?"

If you love the brutal combat system of old-school God of War and the puzzle-filled dungeon structure of The Legend of Zelda, Darksiders is for you. Warmastered Edition brings this legendary beginning back with visuals worthy of modern systems.

Pros:

Visual Improvements: Texture resolution has been doubled, shadows have been sharpened, and 4K support has been added. It still looks quite vibrant for a 2010 game.

Smooth Gameplay: 60 FPS support (and the ability to exceed it) makes combat mechanics much more responsive and enjoyable. Cutting down enemies with War's sword, Chaoseater, is more satisfying than ever.

 A Great Blend of Genres: The game isn't just "hack and slash"; its dungeon designs, platforming elements, and environmental puzzles add incredible depth.

Art Design: The character and world design by comic book artist Joe Madureira is simply iconic. War might be one of the most charismatic game characters ever.

Cons:

Synchronization Issues in Cutscenes: Some players still experience audio and video synchronization issues in cutscenes, which can slightly detract from the atmosphere.

Old-Generation Feel: Some mechanics (especially certain platforming sections and camera angles) show the game's age and can sometimes feel clunky.

No New Features: This isn't a "remake," it's a "remaster." This means that compared to the original game, no new missions or weapons have been added; only technical polishing has been done.

Technical Condition (as of 2026):

Much more stable than the original version.  Especially the ultra-wide screen support and its seamless recognition of modern controllers (DualSense, Xbox, etc.) are huge pluses. It runs quite well even on older computers.

Conclusion:

Darksiders Warmastered Edition is a classic that will make you say, "Why didn't I play this sooner?" If you want to be one of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse and wreak havoc on the world, this is one of the most satisfying action-adventure experiences you can get at this price.

Darksiders plays like Prince of Persia: Sands of Time and Devil May Cry had a baby, on a budget. It's mostly linear, has a story, there's a bunch of platforming and puzzles, and there's a lot of combat where you hack and slash through things with combos. None of it's as slick as the aforementioned games, but it gets close enough to be fun.

Despite being the oldest game in the franchise, Darksiders Warmastered Edition is the least problematic of the lot. It plays great on ultrawide displays, there's a RenoDX mod for great HDR, and I didn't run into any crashes or notable bugs. It's also the only Darksiders game without major perspective issues, as it has a FOV slider unlike 2 and 3 and doesn't have whatever wonky perspective Genesis pretends to be using.

The main issue during gameplay are the controls. They're fine for the most part, but certain segments are very rough. Anything to do with aiming is a nightmare with a controller, but trivial with mouse and keyboard. Unfortunately the engine doesn't support both inputs at once, so switching for one of those wonky aim segments requires restarting the game. I toughed the forced aiming segments out using the controller, but it was frustrating.

Aside from that the only other problems Darksiders has are weak writing and presentation of the story, as well as a terrible audio implementation particularly for cutscenes. The storytelling is improved retroactively by Darksiders 2 and both the gameplay and style the game has are enough to carry it through. As for the audio: prepare to hear dialogue and only dialogue. Music and sound effects are tuned so low during cutscenes they might as well be inaudible. A shame, because the music is actually pretty good. This audio issue is also present in Darksiders 2 and seems to be an engine problem. It's possible that playing with full surround speakers might resolve this, but any stereo or headphone user will have the same issues during cutscenes. Gameplay audio is generally fine.

If you're looking for a solid action-platformer, this is pretty much that. And while the "sequels" are much more problematic in various ways, they both have their charms as well.

[h1]Story[/h1]

You are War, one of the four horsemen of the Apocalypse. You were summoned by the mysterious counsel to keep the balance between Angels and Demons as the End Times approach and menace to destroy the balance of the Universe. 

[h1]Graphics[/h1]

For me, the graphics were a high point in this game. The design of the main characters and antagonists are obviously based on Blizzard games, such as World of Warcraft. The armors and weapons are gigantic, make the small heads of the characters look even smaller. Everything is cartoonish and exaggerated, as in a good comic book.

[h1]Exploration[/h1]

This game has a huge world, separated in large areas, like a cemetery, a deserted city, etc; which you will visit at least twice to complete the game. Some people say it has a “Zelda-like” exploration system, because as you search for you way in the map, you will find chests containing items which will improve you character health and other status. It’s a semi RPG system, in which you have to explore the map in order to make you char more powerful.

[h1]Combat[/h1]

The combat feels like a “heavier” version of Devil May Cry, where each sword swing is slowish but damaging, which makes sense since the main char uses a sword bigger than himself. You can do different moves by pressing different directions as you press the attack button, you can hold the button to throw the enemy in the air, so you can jump and combo him airborne. You know, the standard hack and slash stuff. You can also use the souls you collect from enemies to buy new moves and combos for your sword, as well as buying new weapons, such as the Death scythe. Personally, I mostly used the regular sword and didn’t care much for other weapons.

[h1]Puzzles[/h1]

Now I must say that this game is very heavy into puzzles. Don’t let the Hack and Slash aspect deceive you: you will spend most of your time here solving puzzles. Even some boss battles are puzzle battles, where you can only defeat the boss if you solve the puzzle. 
As you progress the game, you will unlock new abilities and weapons, all of which are essential to solving the many puzzles along the way. The pacing of the game goes like this: exploration-battle-puzzle. Don’t be ashamed to look for guides on the net as some puzzles are really tricky to solve.

[u]The Bad:[/u]

The last dungeon in the game is not only the longest one in the game, but it’s home to the most difficult enemies in the game, and the boss isn’t one of them.

Do yourself a favor and adjust the FOV in the advanced options to your liking so you're not looking at War's backside the entire game.

[b]Story[/b]:

"Deceived by the forces of evil into prematurely bringing about the end of the world, War – the first Horseman of the Apocalypse – stands accused of breaking the sacred law by inciting a war between Heaven and Hell. In the slaughter that ensued, the demonic forces defeated the heavenly hosts and laid claim to the Earth."

The story is well told and pretty straightforward until the end. The characters have nice dialogues even though war sometimes sound cheesy as hell. But it kinda suits its whole honorable persona. [b]Graphics[/b]:

The art direction was done by Joe Madureira and I personally like it a lot. It has a very comic book feel to it and the character designs are very well though. Though I wish the enemy designs were done a little better. The environments are varied and have their own feel to them. You can easily recognize the area just by looking around which is great. Makes sure it doesn't feel stale at any point. Overall a very good looking game.

[b]Sound[/b]:

The sound was okay. The voices are done nicely and the overall feel to the game especially the sword swinging, enemies moaning and War grunting are very nicely done. I couldn't find anything memorable and they are just there just for the sake of being there.

Especially towards the second half of the game, there are some tedious ones but I don't mind them that much. Others might not have the same opinion. The boss battles, for the most part, are great and they all have different methods of defeating them. My personal favorite being the Stygian and Destroyer. 

[b]Overal[/b]l:

I never expected to live this game as much as I did. In fact, I loved it so much that I started a new file right after beating it. Darksiders is a unique and satisfying adventure through a post-apocalyptic, gothic world.

Story: The story is interesting once you understand what's going on. With that said, you don't really understand the story too much the first time through (at least I didn't). But if you take the time to play it again or read some information online the story is quite expansive and compelling. To summarize, you play as War, who seeks to discover the entity responsible for humanity's early extinction. That's as much as I'll say. Wouldn't want to spoil anything.

Graphics: The graphics are okay. I personally like the aesthetic. It combines dark, gothic vibes with somewhat cartoonish looks. It's definitely a cool concept. If you want great graphics, then maybe this isn't your game. But again, graphics really shouldn't determine what makes a great game.

Sound and Music: The soundtrack is beautiful and fits the game perfectly. No track ever sounds like it's out of place. The same goes for the sound effects. The voice acting is great, the sound of your sword slicing through foes is extremely satisfying, and enemies make their presence known through growls, screams or roars. Zero complaints for the sound and music.

Controls: The controls are very much like a God of War. Most people claim that this game ripped off GoW controls, but no game nor company "owns" a control setup, so people need to like the game for what it is and not for what it supposedly tries to be. The controls are easy to learn, cleverly set up, and are fun to use. Also, I recommend you use a controller for this game. 

Gameplay: Much like God of War, the game focuses on combat and puzzle solving -- along with dope boss battles and quick time events. However, unlike God of War, Darksiders is very much like an open world. Like in Zelda, you can visit old areas to discover new things when you have newer equipment. You can also travel and fight by horse throughout the game. You upgrade weapons with souls you and you can unlock special moves in the store. You can find health and magic in chests scattered throughout the world, and you can also find items that will increase these attributes as well. Also, there are different levels of difficulty for gamers of all ranges. The gameplay is great.

Verdict: 8.5
The story isn't exactly told the most coherent or rational way but it is there if you are willing to take a closer look. The aesthetic of the game is enjoyable, the controls are simple but fun, and the gameplay allows for satisfying combat, exploration and puzzle solving. The story could have been depicted more clearly, but Darksiders is still a good game.

I bought the “Darksiders” trilogy (Couldn’t get Genesis) back in July 2021. At first glance I said, 10$ dollars for 3 games sounds like a good deal. After completing each game I can proudly say, all I can say to the franchise’s community is, “Aren’t we making a mighty ruckus?”. 

Darksiders 1 was an experience I loved through and through. I fell deeply for War’s direct yet serene personality to most of the cast you meet in the game. A warrior with only respect for arms and combat, while retaining his cunningness during the fights and his analytical understanding in the story. With the same voice as Gaara from Naruto DUB and Asura in Asura’s Wrath, Liam O'Brien, the story of the warmaster was perfectly introduced and portrayed. 

The narrative and the cast  of the Darksiders played their roles in the best way possible. I was shocked with some of the plot twists that explained the course of War’s Adventure. I gasped a lot. Most cutscenes and in-game dialogue explained most of the rules and concepts of this fictional universe. The theme of The Four Riders of the Apocalypse was adapted rather impressively. 

As a “Hack ‘n Slash” fan and Puzzle Solver enthusiast, I was astonished with the core gameplay mechanics of War’s Movement Set. I found it to be a bit clunky at times. Even though it was basic and simple moves, they felt powerful and refined, similar to the personality of the warmaster himself. The combat always felt thrilling when facing the hordes of hell. However,the enemy AI was dumb sometimes. They either stood frozen in place for you to hit them. Others died walking backwards into a death wall, a cliff or as soon as they spawned. The Bosses were executed greatly, both figuratively and literally. They used the same mechanics the player learned throughout his journey, while retaining the “HIT THE THING AND KILL IT” vibe.  

The puzzle sections are recursive gimmicks throughout the franchise. They require a bit of thinking and attention regarding your current arsenal and location. They always give enough clues for you to figure out what to do and where to go next. As for the landscapes, environments and level designs, they were carefully planned and detailed. The diabolical dungeons you explore through a dystopian earth are polished beautifully. 

Even though it’s graphics cannot compare to other titles that were published in the same period, it is a great game and entry in the action H&S genre. Many people see it as a God Of War Rip-Off, but that is just a formula for this type of project. Nowadays making something completely original is complicated. 

But what you can do is take the formula of a specific genre and adapt it to your own vision, guidelines and themes. And I believe the devs at Kaiko and Vigil Games did exactly that. As a result, it made a great start for the Darksiders Universe. A game for gamers made by gamers. 8.5/10
